title: Let my people go
teaser: Day 39 of Bible 365 — Exodus 7-11. The plagues are not tantrums. They are God walking down the list of Egypt's gods, one by one, and proving each one empty.

emphasis: so that they may worship Me
there is no one like Me in all the earth
judgment against all the gods of Egypt
modules.passage: Then say to him, "The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to tell you: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness. But you have not listened until now." ... Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD says: 'Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.'" ... "I will send all My plagues against you and your officials and your people, so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth." ... "On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male, both man and beast, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD."

modules.meaning: send away My people; release My people; let My people go
modules.rootMeaning: Shalach is the ordinary Hebrew verb for sending, releasing, letting go - the word you use to set a bird loose or send a servant away free. Ammi is 'My people.' God does not ask Pharaoh to be kind to slaves. He claims them as His own and demands they be released to Him.
modules.usageNote: The demand returns six times across these chapters (7:16; 8:1; 8:20; 9:1; 9:13; 10:3), and it is never the whole sentence. Every time it is followed by a purpose: 'so that they may worship Me.' The freedom God commands is not freedom for its own sake. It is freedom from one master in order to belong to another.

wordByWord.meaning: send away, release, let go (an intensive imperative - 'release them, and mean it')
the marker that points to the direct object - here, the ones being released
My people - the suffix '-i' makes the claim personal: they are Mine
so that they may serve/worship Me - the same root used for the slavery they are leaving

relatedWords.reference: The verb behind 'worship Me' (veya'avduni) is the same root as the 'hard labor' Israel performed for Pharaoh in Exodus 1:13-14. Israel will not stop serving. They will change masters - from a king who works them to death to a God who works them into life.

modules.definition: to send, send away, let go, release
modules.usage: Pharaoh keeps trying to negotiate the terms - go, but leave your children; go, but leave your flocks. God keeps refusing. The release He commands is total, because a people only partly freed are not free at all.

modules.heading: Ten Blows, Ten Verdicts
modules.body:
It is easy to read Exodus 7 through 11 as a contest of stubbornness - Pharaoh says no, God turns up the pressure, Pharaoh says no again. Read that way, the plagues can feel like an escalating tantrum, a heavenly arm-twist until the human king finally gives in.

But that is not how the book itself explains them. The plagues have a stated purpose, and it is repeated so many times you cannot miss it: "so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth" (9:14). "In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land" (8:22). "By this you will know that I am the LORD" (7:17). These are not pressure tactics. They are revelations. Each one is teaching somebody something true about who God is.

And here is the part that turns the whole passage on its head. The plagues are aimed. Egypt was a land thick with gods. The Nile was worshiped as the god Hapi, source of all life - so the first plague turns the Nile to blood. The frog was sacred to the goddess Heqet - so the land heaves with frogs until they rot in stinking heaps. Ra the sun god, the highest god in Egypt's sky, the one Pharaoh claimed as his own father - so a darkness that can be felt swallows the sun for three days. The book tells us plainly what is happening: "I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt" (12:12). The plagues are God walking down the list of everything Egypt trusted instead of Him, and crossing each one off.
modules.keyInsight: The plagues are not God losing patience. They are God conducting a trial - putting every false god of Egypt in the dock and exposing it as empty. The point is never just freedom for Israel. The point is that there is no one like the LORD in all the earth.

modules.heading: The Things She Could Not Take Out of the House
modules.body:
A woman I know spent two years getting out from under a man who controlled her. By the time she left, the danger was not really him anymore. He had moved three states away. The danger was the house itself - the rooms full of objects that still ran her life from the inside.

The phone she could not stop checking. The scale in the bathroom she stepped on every morning before she let herself eat. The closet organized to his taste. The bank app she opened a dozen times a day, certain that money was the thing that would finally make her safe. She was free on paper. She was still a servant in fact, and the masters were small gods she had carried out of the old life and set up quietly in the new one.

Her counselor did not tell her to feel better about herself. She did something stranger. One by one, she made the woman name each thing out loud and say what it had promised her - safety, control, worth, love - and then say plainly what it had actually delivered. The phone promised connection and gave her dread. The scale promised control and gave her hunger. It was slow and it was not gentle. But naming each false promise for what it was is exactly how the chains came off. You cannot leave a god you will not admit you are serving.
modules.connectionToTheme: Israel had to watch every Egyptian god fail in public before they could believe there was no one like the LORD. We rarely leave our small gods until we have watched each one fail to deliver what it swore.

modules.heading: Even the Magicians Saw It
modules.body:
Watch the slow collapse of Egypt's own experts. For the first two plagues, Pharaoh's magicians keep pace - they turn their staffs to serpents, they conjure frogs. The contest looks even.

Then the third plague comes, the dust of the earth becomes gnats, and the magicians try and fail. And it is they, not Moses, who say the decisive sentence: "This is the finger of God" (8:19). The people whose whole job was defending Egypt's gods are the first to confess they have met a power their gods cannot match.

Notice what the text says happens next. Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen. The evidence was overwhelming and admitted out loud by his own staff - and still he would not let go. This is the sober thing the plagues reveal about the human heart. Proof is not the problem. We can watch our gods fail in real time, hear the experts admit it, feel the cost of our stubbornness mount, and still refuse to release what we are clutching. Pharaoh is not stupid. He is a portrait of what it looks like to know and not bow.
modules.historicalContext: Egyptian magicians (the term in 8:19 refers to ritual specialists of the royal court) were not stage performers but learned priests whose role was to maintain cosmic order through sacred rites. For these men to declare 'the finger of God' was an admission that the gods they served had been overpowered by a foreign God they did not recognize - a stunning concession from inside the system itself.
modules.fascinatingFact: From the third plague onward, the text repeatedly stresses that God makes a distinction (8:22-23; 9:26; 11:7): the flies, the hail, the darkness, the death of the firstborn all fall on Egypt while Goshen, where Israel lived, is spared. The plagues do not only judge false gods; they separate, drawing a visible line between those who belong to the LORD and those who do not - 'not even a dog will snarl' at Israel (11:7).

modules.ancientTruth: Through ten plagues God puts the gods of Egypt on trial and exposes every one - the Nile-god, the frog-goddess, the sun-god, the divine Pharaoh himself - as powerless. 'I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD' (Exodus 12:12).
modules.modernApplication: We do not bow to Hapi or Ra, but we serve their grandchildren: the bank balance that promises safety, the body that promises worth, the achievement that promises a name, the screen that promises we are never alone. Each one runs us the way Egypt's gods ran Egypt, and each one fails to deliver what it swore. God still walks down the list, in mercy, exposing each false god so we will stop trusting it.
modules.connectionPoint: The demand of these chapters - 'Let My people go, so that they may worship Me' - is never satisfied by mere release. Israel is not freed into open desert to do as they please; they are freed to serve the God who claimed them. Salvation, in the Bible's grammar, is always a transfer of ownership: out of the house of slavery, into the household of God.
modules.newTestamentEcho: What the plagues began, the cross completed. Paul says that at Calvary God 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and 'made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them' (Colossians 2:15) - the same public unmasking of every false power, now final. And the cry 'Let My people go' finds its deepest answer in the Son: 'So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed' (John 8:36). Christ is the greater Exodus, leading not one nation out of one empire but a people out of slavery to sin and death.

modules.prompt: Which small god in your life is God patiently exposing right now - the thing you keep trusting to deliver safety, worth, or control, that keeps failing to?
additionalQuestions: Pharaoh's own magicians admitted 'the finger of God,' and he still would not let go. Where have you already seen the evidence that something cannot save you - and clutched it anyway?
God commands not just freedom but freedom 'so that they may worship Me.' If God set you free from your biggest attachment tomorrow, what would He be freeing you for?
Pharaoh kept offering partial releases - go, but leave the children; go, but leave the flocks. What partial surrender are you offering God instead of the whole thing?

modules.prayerText: LORD, God of the Hebrews, there is no one like You in all the earth. You see the gods I have carried into my freedom - the ones I keep trusting to make me safe, to make me enough, to keep me from being alone. One by one, expose them. Let me watch them fail and not run back to them. I confess the Pharaoh in me, the part that has seen the proof and still will not let go. Soften what is hard. Then say over me what You said over Israel: let My people go, so that they may worship Me. Free me into Yourself. Amen.

modules.commitment: Name one small god today - out loud, the way the woman in the story did. Say what it promised you and what it has actually delivered. Then hand that one thing to God and ask Him to be, for you, the thing it could never be.
leavingAtCross: The false gods I have carried out of my old life and quietly set up in the new one
The Pharaoh-stubbornness that sees the evidence and still refuses to release
The lie that I am free when I have only changed which master owns me
receivingFromCross: A God who walks down the list of my idols in mercy, not to shame me but to free me
Freedom that is not emptiness but belonging - released, so that I may worship Him
The triumph of Christ, who disarmed every power that held me and set me free indeed
modules.content: Name one small god today - out loud, the way the woman in the story did. Say what it promised you and what it has actually delivered. Then hand that one thing to God and ask Him to be, for you, the thing it could never be.

forReflection: According to the passage itself, what is the stated purpose of the plagues - and how does that differ from reading them as God merely pressuring Pharaoh?
What does Exodus 12:12 reveal the plagues were really aimed at, and why does that change how you read the whole sequence?
The demand is always 'Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.' Why does that second half matter - what is freedom for?
forAccountabilityPartners: Name one 'small god' you have been serving - something that promises safety, worth, or control and keeps failing to deliver.
Talk about your inner Pharaoh: where have you seen clear evidence that something cannot save you, and refused to let it go anyway?
Ask each other: if God set you free from your biggest attachment, what do you think He would be setting you free for?

relatedScriptures.text: "This is the finger of God," the magicians said to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.
And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.
So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.

forDeeperStudy.title: Exodus 7-11
forDeeperStudy.note: Read the plague cycle in one sitting, tracking two things: how often God states 'so that you may know,' and how Pharaoh's heart is described after each plague. Watch the proof mount and the refusal harden together.

modules.name: Pharaoh
modules.title: The King Who Would Not Let Go
modules.description: The unnamed ruler of Egypt, regarded by his people as a living god and the earthly son of Ra. Across the plague cycle he becomes the great contrast to the LORD: where God reveals Himself to be known and worshiped, Pharaoh hardens himself again and again, even after his own priests confess defeat. He is not a fool brought down by ignorance but a will brought down by refusal - the human heart in close-up, choosing its grip over its freedom.
modules.keyQuote: Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.
modules.lessonForUs: Pharaoh proves that knowledge is never the real obstacle. He sees the finger of God, hears the experts admit it, watches his gods fail one by one - and still will not release what he is clutching. The question the plagues press on us is not 'Have you seen enough?' but 'Will you let go?'
modules.heading: The King Who Would Not Let Go

sources: Scripture quotations from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), public domain.
Hebrew word study (shallach et-ammi, H7971; the avad / 'serve-worship' wordplay shared with Israel's slavery in Exodus 1:13-14) reflects standard lexical sources.

The identification of specific plagues with specific Egyptian deities (Hapi with the Nile, Heqet with the frog, Ra with the sun) reflects a long-standing reading grounded in the text's own claim that God would 'execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt' (Exodus 12:12); precise one-to-one mappings of every plague are debated among scholars.
